content.thinking:
The user just asked me to check the progress of the 2B training run, and once it finishes I need to record the scores, update the journal, commit, and report final results with leaderboard placement. I already have a monitor set up that will push events like “training done” or “final results” as they appear in the log, but the user is explicitly requesting a manual check right now. 

From the most recent log excerpt I fetched, the training is at 84% (1.68G/2.00G tokens) with an estimated 2 hours remaining. That means the run is still ongoing, so there are no final scores yet. However, to prepare for when it finishes I should start gathering any intermediate artifacts that will be needed later: the checkpoint directories that are being written to disk and any recent step lines that could indicate the latest checkpoint or a possible OOM. 

I know the training script writes checkpoints under `runs/<run_id>/checkpoints/`. The most recent run directory can be identified by listing `runs/` sorted by modification time (`ls -t`). Then I can list its `checkpoints/` subdirectory to see what checkpoint files exist. This will be useful later when I need to extract the best checkpoint name for evaluation.

Additionally, the log file may contain step lines like “step 123456” or OOM warnings that are not part of the regular progress bar output (which includes “tok/s”). By converting carriage returns to newlines (`tr '\\r' '\\n'`) and grepping for “step” or “oom” while excluding the “tok/s” lines, I can quickly see the most recent step numbers or any OOM events. Limiting to the first few matches (`head -5`) keeps the output concise.

Putting this together, the appropriate command is a Bash one that:
1. Lists the contents of `runs/` to see available run folders.
2. Lists the checkpoints inside the most recent run folder (`ls runs/$(ls -t runs/ | head -1)/checkpoints/`), suppressing errors if the folder doesn’t exist yet.
3. Extracts recent step or OOM lines from the log, after normalizing line endings, and filters out the noisy “tok/s” progress lines.

This will give me a snapshot of the on‑disk state and any recent step information, which I can later use to decide when the run is complete and to locate the final checkpoint for evaluation. Hence I will issue the Bash tool call with exactly that command.

arguments.command: ls runs/; ls runs/$(ls -t runs/ | head -1)/checkpoints/ 2>/dev/null; tr '\r' '\n' < /tmp/mythos_2b_run.log | grep -iE "step|oom" | grep -v "tok/s" | head -5
arguments.description: Check checkpoints on disk and any step lines
